summary: Argus is a mission-planning tool for NASA Space Apps Challenge. It helps planners identify Earth locations that resemble landing or experiment sites on the Moon or Mars. Users describe requirements in chat or upload a specification. Argus turns those details into structured site drafts and compares locations using terrain, climate, geology, solar availability, and mineral composition. Ranked analogs appear on an interactive 3D globe, with terrain views for closer inspection. Workspaces keep missions and conversations organized, while reports help teams share findings. Configurable priorities and AI-assisted workflows make early site assessment more accessible and transparent for mission planning teams everywhere.
details:
Argus is an AI-powered planetary analog site discovery and mission-planning platform designed to help researchers identify locations on Earth that resemble extraterrestrial environments, particularly potential landing and exploration sites on the Moon and Mars.

The core idea behind Argus is that understanding other planets can begin by studying environments on our own planet. Earth contains numerous geological and environmental analogs of extraterrestrial landscapes, but identifying, comparing, and evaluating these locations requires analyzing large amounts of scientific and environmental data.

Argus addresses this challenge through an AI-assisted workflow. Users can describe their mission objectives and environmental requirements through a conversational interface or upload a mission specification. The system transforms these requirements into structured criteria, identifies potential terrestrial analog sites, and evaluates them based on their similarity to the target planetary environment. Results are organized into candidate site profiles and presented through an interactive 3D globe and terrain visualizations, allowing users to explore locations and compare their characteristics.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Argus aims to make preliminary planetary site assessment faster, more accessible, and more systematic. Instead of manually investigating different datasets and comparing locations across separate platforms, researchers can explore relevant environmental factors in one workspace. This can help scientists identify promising terrestrial analogs, evaluate trade-offs between candidate locations, and better prepare for future planetary exploration missions.

Our long-term vision is to support planetary scientists, mission planners, and researchers by making Earth-based analog research more accessible and data-driven. Argus is designed as a preliminary research and decision-support tool rather than a replacement for expert geological analysis or mission-specific validation.

Technology and Development

We developed Argus using Next.js, React, and TypeScript. The interface is built with OpenUI, while the interactive 3D globe and geographical visualizations use react-globe.gl and Three.js.

For its AI workflow, Argus supports local inference through Ollama, alongside optional cloud-based and Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) configurations. Our AI research also explores domain specialization through the LFM3-1.7B language model and supervised fine-tuning using space-science and geoscience-oriented datasets, including Astronomy, Stack Exchange Space Q&A, and GeoGPT-QA. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a way to ground scientific responses in relevant NASA documentation and research materials.

The environmental data workflow incorporates NASA POWER climatological data and Open-Meteo elevation information, alongside other relevant terrain and planetary science parameters.

Scientific Factors Considered

Our team considered multiple dimensions when evaluating terrestrial analog environments:

  • Temperature and climatological conditions
  • Elevation and topographical characteristics
  • Solar availability and exposure
  • Radiation proxies
  • Aridity and environmental extremes
  • Geological characteristics
  • Mineralogical composition
  • Terrain morphology and surface roughness

We chose these factors because planetary analog identification requires more than simply finding locations that look visually similar. Environmental, geological, and mineralogical characteristics must also be considered to establish meaningful scientific comparisons.

Creativity and Innovation

What makes Argus distinctive is its combination of conversational AI, structured environmental analysis, scientific data retrieval, and interactive geospatial visualization in a unified platform.

Rather than treating planetary analog discovery as a simple geographical search, Argus approaches it as a multi-criteria scientific matching problem. Users can communicate mission requirements naturally, explore candidate locations spatially, and investigate the reasoning behind different site comparisons.

Ultimately, Argus aims to bridge the gap between Earth observation and planetary exploration, turning our planet into a practical research environment for understanding worlds beyond it.
